pages.text: Sundiata: the Full Epic

image.note: Cover: a griot with a kora, a young king rising

pages.text: Contents. The Prophecy / The Child Who Could Not Walk / Sundiata Rises / Exile / The Sorcerer-King / The Battle of Kirina / The Empire of Mali.

This is one of the greatest stories of Africa, told for eight hundred years by the griots, the keepers of memory, who pass it from voice to voice. It is the story of Sundiata, the boy who could not walk, who rose to build the mighty empire of Mali.

image.note: A griot playing a kora, telling the tale

pages.text: Long ago in the land of Mali, a hunter came before the king with a prophecy. "A great king will come after you," he said, "greater than any before. But he will be born of a plain and humble woman, a stranger. Marry her, and your name will live for ever through her son."

image.note: A hunter foretelling before the king

pages.text: Soon after, two hunters brought to the court a woman named Sogolon, plain of face and hunched of back, and strange in her ways. She was not beautiful, and the court laughed behind their hands. But the king remembered the prophecy, and he married her, and waited.

image.note: Sogolon arriving at court, courtiers whispering

pages.text: In time Sogolon bore a son, and he was named Sundiata. The whole kingdom watched this child of prophecy, the boy who was meant to be the greatest king of all. But as the years passed, a heavy worry grew. For Sundiata could not walk.

image.note: Baby Sundiata, the court watching closely

chapters.title: The Child Who Could Not Walk

pages.text: At three years old, he crawled. At five, he crawled still. At seven, while other boys ran and wrestled, Sundiata dragged himself along the ground on his strong arms, silent and watchful, and could not stand. The prophecy, people whispered, had surely been a lie.

image.note: Young Sundiata crawling as other boys run

pages.text: How they mocked him, and worse, how they mocked his mother. The king's other wife, jealous for her own son, laughed loudest of all. "So this is the great king?" she sneered at Sogolon. "A boy who eats the dust. You and your crawling son." And Sogolon wept alone, for her boy's sake.

image.note: The jealous queen sneering at Sogolon

pages.text: The old king died, and though he had wished Sundiata to follow him, the jealous queen seized the throne for her own son instead, and Sundiata and his mother were pushed aside, poor and scorned. It seemed the boy of prophecy would come to nothing at all.

image.note: The jealous queen's son taking the throne

pages.text: One day the cruel queen refused Sogolon even a handful of baobab leaves for her cooking pot, and jeered, "Send your son to fetch them, if he can stand." Sogolon came home in tears and, for the first time, poured out to her silent son all the shame they bore.

image.note: Sogolon weeping before Sundiata

pages.text: Something rose in Sundiata then. "Mother," he said quietly, "today I will walk." He sent for the blacksmiths to forge the heaviest iron bar in all the land. Six strong men carried it to him. And before the watching people, Sundiata took hold of it, and began to pull himself up.

image.note: Blacksmiths carrying a great iron bar

pages.text: The iron bar bent like a bow in his hands, but Sundiata rose. Trembling, sweating, roaring with the effort of years, the boy who had never stood pushed himself onto his feet, straightened his back, and stood tall at last before them all. The crowd fell silent, then gasped, then cheered.

image.note: Sundiata rising, bending the iron bar

pages.text: Then, upright, he walked, slow and steady, to the great baobab tree, put his arms around its trunk, and pulled the whole tree from the earth. He carried it back and set it down at his mother's door. "Now, Mother," he said, "you need never beg for leaves again." The prophecy had woken at last.

image.note: Sundiata carrying an uprooted baobab tree

pages.text: But a hero who suddenly stands tall makes his enemies afraid. The jealous queen, seeing Sundiata's strength and the people's love for him, plotted against his life. To keep him safe, Sogolon took her son and left Mali, into a long exile in distant lands.

image.note: Sundiata and Sogolon leaving Mali

pages.text: For years they wandered, guests in foreign courts, and Sundiata grew into a young man, tall and strong and wise. He learned the arts of war and of kingship, made friends and allies, and never forgot his home. He was waiting, though he did not yet know for what.

image.note: Sundiata as a young warrior in a foreign court

pages.text: While Sundiata was away, a terror fell upon Mali. A sorcerer-king named Soumaoro, cruel and powerful, conquered the land. It was said he had a secret chamber of dark and terrible magic, and that no ordinary weapon could harm him. The people of Mali suffered, and despaired.

image.note: The sorcerer-king Soumaoro on a dark throne

pages.text: In their misery, the people remembered the boy of prophecy. Messengers were sent across the world to find Sundiata, and at last they knelt before him. "Come home," they begged. "Only you can free us. Mali is dying, and you are its rightful king." Sundiata rose. "Then I will come," he said.

image.note: Messengers kneeling before Sundiata

pages.text: Sundiata gathered his armies from all the friends and allies he had made in exile, and marched home to Mali. Soumaoro came out to meet him with a mighty host, and the two great powers faced each other at last on the field of Kirina.

image.note: Two armies facing across the field of Kirina

pages.text: But how do you defeat a king that no weapon can wound? Sundiata had learned the sorcerer's secret. Soumaoro's power could be undone by the spur of a white rooster, fixed to an arrow. In the thick of the battle, Sundiata loosed that single arrow, and it struck home.

image.note: Sundiata drawing a special arrow

pages.text: The moment it touched him, Soumaoro's magic drained away. His power was broken, his army scattered, and the sorcerer-king fled into the mountains and was never seen again. The long nightmare was over. On the field of Kirina, Sundiata had won back his land.

image.note: Soumaoro's power breaking, his army fleeing

pages.text: The freed peoples came together and made Sundiata their king, their Mansa, and more than that: they joined their many lands under him into one great realm. That day the empire of Mali was born, and Sundiata, the boy who could not walk, was its first and greatest ruler.

image.note: Sundiata crowned Mansa, the peoples gathered

pages.text: Under Sundiata, Mali grew rich and wide and peaceful. He gave it wise laws, and a great charter that spoke of the dignity of every person, remembered to this day. From this empire would come, in time, gold and learning famous across the whole world.

image.note: The Mali Empire flourishing

pages.text: And the boy once mocked in the dust became the hero every griot sings. For eight hundred years his story has passed from voice to voice, telling children a truth worth keeping: that the one the world counts out may yet rise the highest of all.

image.note: A griot singing to children under a tree

pages.text: People to remember. Sundiata: the boy who could not walk, and became the first ruler of Mali. Sogolon: his mother, who never lost hope. Soumaoro: the sorcerer-king he defeated. The griots: the storytellers who have kept this tale alive for eight hundred years.

image.note: A gallery: Sundiata, Sogolon, a griot

pages.text: Sundiata's Mali would grow into one of the richest empires the world has ever known. But that is a story for the history books. This one, the griots would say, is truer than history: for it is not only what happened, but what it means.
